title: Leap Day

jokes.text: I've had my skin tags removed since then so you can see my eyes now.
jokes.setup: Thad is reintroducing himself to Liz from college, trying to jog her memory
jokes.punchline: The detail that skin tags were previously obscuring his eyes — delivered as a casual identifier
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly specific and grotesque. The image of skin tags covering someone's eyes is wildly original, delivered with total deadpan normalcy. It instantly and economically establishes Thad as a memorably pathetic figure. The specificity earns it — this isn't a generic nerd joke, it's a precise, disgusting visual detail used as a casual social icebreaker.

jokes.text: Thank you, no everyone thinks of the young Nazi boy as the star of that show.
jokes.setup: Liz points out that Thad was the star of The Sound of Music
jokes.punchline: Thad sarcastically 'thanks' her while noting that everyone defaults to thinking of Rolf, the young Nazi boy, as the star
jokes.explanation: A neat subversion — framing 'the young Nazi boy' as a neutral theatrical descriptor is darkly funny. The joke works because of what Thad is NOT saying: he's offended to be overshadowed by a Nazi. Solid economy and a genuine laugh.

jokes.text: A lot of people didn't realize that was the free, unlicensed version.
jokes.setup: Thad is reminiscing about their college production of The Sound of Music
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions it was an unlicensed production, as though that's a minor footnote
jokes.explanation: A quick throwaway that rewards attention — the idea of a free, unlicensed Sound of Music is absurd but totally plausible for a broke college theater group. Good economy, solid chuckle.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz, new Bluetooth? / No, I'm talking to someone. / I'm sorry. I don't see people that look like that.
jokes.setup: Jenna sees Liz apparently talking to no one and assumes she has a Bluetooth earpiece
jokes.punchline: When Liz clarifies she's talking to a real person, Jenna says she 'doesn't see people that look like that' — revealing her total superficiality/looks-based worldview
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Jenna — she literally does not register unattractive people as people. The joke's structure is clean: misread, correction, devastating reveal about Jenna's character. Could only work with Jenna delivering it.

jokes.text: That was this creep I went to college with. Such a nerd. And this is coming from someone who wrote lyrics to the song the cantina band plays in Star Wars.
jokes.setup: Liz dismisses Thad as a nerd
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts her own dismissal by admitting she wrote lyrics to the Star Wars cantina song
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon self-own. The specificity of 'wrote lyrics to the cantina band song' is inspired — it's not just a Star Wars reference, it's the particular act of writing LYRICS to an INSTRUMENTAL. It's deeply nerdy in the most Liz Lemon way possible. High character integration, great economy, very quotable.

jokes.text: No, that was sad Thad the skintag lad. I coined that.
jokes.setup: Pete suggests the guy Liz was talking to was Thad Warmald the billionaire
jokes.punchline: Liz insists he's 'sad Thad the skintag lad' — a rhyming nickname she proudly claims coinage of
jokes.explanation: A callback that pays off the earlier skin tag detail with a catchy rhyming nickname. 'I coined that' is delivered with misplaced pride, which is funny. The rhyme scheme is genuinely satisfying.

jokes.text: I don't know a lot about business, but he did an Internet and now the computers like him and Wall Street is Google.
jokes.setup: Pete explains Thad is a billionaire tech entrepreneur
jokes.punchline: Jenna's summary of his success: 'he did an Internet and now the computers like him and Wall Street is Google'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Jenna's attempt to summarize tech business is grammatically and logically scrambled in a way that feels like genuine Jenna logic — not just random stupidity but a specific kind of celebrity-brained garbling. 'He did an Internet' is superb. 'Wall Street is Google' is inspired nonsense that somehow tracks as a mistake someone would make. Extremely quotable, perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Liz, I'm on a sexual walkabout right now. I need to know if anything can make me happier than being with Paul. And maybe $20 billion would do it.
jokes.setup: Liz is reluctant to go to Thad's party
jokes.punchline: Jenna reveals she's on a 'sexual walkabout' and wonders if $20 billion could top her boyfriend Paul
jokes.explanation: 'Sexual walkabout' is a great coinage — the term implies spiritual self-discovery applied to sexual exploration. Very on-brand for Jenna. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Poke your eye, pull your hair, you forgot what clothes to wear.
jokes.setup: Liz isn't wearing yellow and blue, the Leap Day colors
jokes.punchline: Kenneth and others recite the Leap Day rhyme for punishment, then physically carry it out
jokes.explanation: Part of the episode's central absurdist conceit — Leap Day as a fully developed alternate holiday with its own rules. The rhyme is catchy and the physical follow-through (poking eyes, pulling hair) escalates it nicely.

jokes.text: He lives in the Mariana trench. He emerges every four years to trade children's tears for candy.
jokes.setup: Liz has never heard of Leap Day William
jokes.punchline: Kenneth describes Leap Day William as a creature from the Mariana Trench who trades children's tears for candy — delivered with total earnest conviction
jokes.explanation: The Leap Day William mythology is this episode's comedic crown jewel. The specificity of 'Mariana Trench,' the deeply disturbing candy-for-tears economy, and Kenneth's complete sincerity make this exceptional. It's a fully realized absurdist world-building joke that parodies holiday mythology (Santa Claus, Tooth Fairy) while being genuinely strange and dark. The writers committed fully to the bit.

jokes.text: But white haven was founded by the Amish, and we really only celebrated their holidays. After high school, I went on rumspringa. It was crazy. I totally snuck into The Witches of Eastwick.
jokes.setup: Liz explains why she doesn't know about Leap Day William
jokes.punchline: Her 'crazy' rumspringa consisted of sneaking into The Witches of Eastwick — the tamest possible rebellion
jokes.explanation: A layered joke: the absurdity of White Haven being Amish-founded, Liz doing rumspringa, and the devastating anticlimax of her 'crazy' rebellion being sneaking into a PG-13 movie. Perfect Liz Lemon characterization — she thinks this is wild. The escalating setup makes the tiny punchline land harder.

jokes.text: Certainly not at a Michael's crafts crafting cruise. / Miss Lemon, you are missing out.
jokes.setup: Jack asks where Liz was four years ago when they last celebrated Leap Day
jokes.punchline: He preemptively denies being on a Michael's crafts cruise (which clearly means he was) and then smoothly pivots
jokes.explanation: The joke is Jack's uncharacteristic defensiveness revealing exactly what he was doing — a Michael's crafts cruise. The specificity of 'crafting cruise' paired with Jack Donaghy's patrician persona is the comedy. The unprompted denial is the tell.

jokes.text: For instance, I am wearing a braided necklace with a shark's tooth on it. I listened to rap music for the first time. Not a fan.
jokes.setup: Jack is encouraging Liz to take a chance on Leap Day — to do things she ordinarily wouldn't
jokes.punchline: His examples of bold Leap Day behavior are a beachy necklace and listening to rap — and he didn't like it
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated Jack Donaghy comedy. His 'wild' Leap Day behavior is comically constrained: a tourist trinket and a genre of music most people encountered in childhood. 'Not a fan' delivered with Alec Baldwin's deadpan is the killer. The joke works entirely because of character — Jack's WASP conservatism makes these mundane acts feel transgressive to him.

jokes.text: Okay, fine, I'll go, but if he has a giant chandelier in his house, I'm out. Those things fall.
jokes.setup: Jack convinces Liz to go to Thad's party
jokes.punchline: Her one dealbreaker condition is chandeliers — because 'those things fall'
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon neurotic practicality. She agrees to a potentially life-changing encounter but draws the line at chandelier risk. The absurdly specific safety concern is very on-brand.

jokes.text: It's not such a big deal in Boston, either. Just a Leap Day William parade, citywide ice maze and we don't poke you in the eye if you're not wearing yellow and blue. We just stomp on your foot. Kick you in the knee, Yankees suck, go Pats.
jokes.setup: Liz is shocked that Leap Day is celebrated everywhere
jokes.punchline: Pete describes Boston's version as slightly less violent eye-poking (just foot-stomping and knee-kicking) before devolving into Boston sports tribalism
jokes.explanation: The regional variation joke works well — Boston's 'milder' version of the holiday still involves physical assault, which is funny. The snap into 'Yankees suck, go Pats' is a perfect Pete character button. Good structure with an escalating list.

jokes.text: Uptight lawyer Dave Williams turns into the real Leap Day William after an ice fishing trip gone awry. USA runs an all-day marathon.
jokes.setup: Pete references the movie 'Leap Dave Williams'
jokes.punchline: The movie is a parody of holiday body-swap films ('Leap Dave Williams' being a play on 'Leap Day William'), and USA Network runs a marathon — a spot-on satire of mid-tier cable holiday programming
jokes.explanation: The writers fully commit to the fake holiday by inventing its associated pop culture: a holiday body-swap movie called 'Leap Dave Williams' that USA runs all day. This is meticulous world-building comedy. The USA Network detail is a perfect, specific satirical touch — exactly the channel that would do this.

jokes.text: Dave, is everything all right? / I definitely don't have gills. I mean, nothing. I mean, yes.
jokes.setup: We hear a clip from the fictional 'Leap Dave Williams' movie
jokes.punchline: The Dave Williams character panics and blurts out 'I definitely don't have gills' — a Freudian slip about his Leap Day William transformation
jokes.explanation: A very well-executed parody of the body-swap genre. The triple correction — 'nothing... yes' — is perfectly structured. The specificity of gills (since Leap Day William lives in the Mariana Trench) rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, that's what Chris kept quoting this morning during our love... making.
jokes.setup: Cerie recognizes the Leap Dave Williams quote being discussed
jokes.punchline: Her boyfriend was quoting it during sex — she trails off awkwardly on 'love...making'
jokes.explanation: The overshare is effective cringe comedy. The pause on 'love...making' adds a nice beat of awkwardness. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Gabe's got the week off. He's a Mormon. You know how they are about Leap Day.
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains why he's filling in as an assistant
jokes.punchline: The real assistant is Mormon and has the week off for Leap Day — implying Mormons have special/serious Leap Day observances, which is pure invented absurdist lore
jokes.explanation: The joke works by layering Leap Day mythology with religious-holiday specificity. Kenneth's 'you know how they are about Leap Day' treats it like Passover or Ramadan. The confident delivery of invented lore is the comedic engine here.

jokes.text: Fine, I didn't wanna have to do this, but I am wearing yellow and blue.
jokes.setup: Jack is being challenged about not wearing Leap Day colors
jokes.punchline: He dramatically reveals his yellow-and-blue outfit underneath — implying he was prepared all along but was holding it in reserve
jokes.explanation: The visual reveal of Jack's yellow-and-blue outfit is funny because it confirms his secret Leap Day enthusiasm despite his patrician exterior. The 'I didn't want to have to do this' framing, as if revealing a secret weapon, is very Jack Donaghy.

jokes.text: Well, certainly you remember the joy that fills a young boy's heart on the day of leap.
jokes.setup: Jack tries to bond with Kenneth over Leap Day before revealing his true mercenary motivation
jokes.punchline: Jack speaks about 'the day of leap' with mock reverence — the grandiose phrasing ('the day of leap') is pompously theatrical
jokes.explanation: The pompous holiday phrasing is mildly funny, setting up the turn to pure capitalism. Works as a setup beat more than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Because it's an extra day to do business. A bonus profit opportunity. I have a bet with my business school roommates every four years to see who can make the most money on Leap Day.
jokes.setup: Jack builds up the spiritual meaning of Leap Day...
jokes.punchline: ...only to reveal his actual reason for loving Leap Day is a money competition with his business school friends
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy misdirection — the setup feigns holiday sentimentality before the punchline pivots to pure capitalist competition. The misdirection structure is clean and the character integration is excellent: only Jack would have an every-four-years profit contest.

jokes.text: It'll be like those Bible quotes are right in your face.
jokes.setup: Jack is announcing the acquisition of Xaro, a 3-D Internet company
jokes.punchline: His example of what 3-D Internet will be like is Bible quotes 'right in your face'
jokes.explanation: A quick, sharp joke about what a conservative Catholic Republican would imagine 3-D Internet is for. The specificity of Bible quotes as his mental model of exciting internet content is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Of course, take off my bald cap. Not put on my wig.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Kenneth to take off his bald cap
jokes.punchline: Kenneth clarifies to himself that this means removing the bald cap, not putting on a wig — implying he has a wig ready and this is a relevant distinction for him
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that implies Kenneth's eccentric costume habits extend further than we know. The joke is in what's NOT said: why does he have a wig on standby? Classic 30 Rock economy.

jokes.text: Well, he's definitely rich. [Liz surveying the apartment]
jokes.setup: Liz and Jenna arrive at Thad's party in what is presumably an extremely lavish apartment
jokes.punchline: Liz's dry observation that he's 'definitely rich' — delivered as if it needed confirming
jokes.explanation: A brief transitional joke. The understatement is Liz-appropriate but it's fairly generic. Works as scene-setting more than a great joke.

jokes.text: Oh, what's that animal? You know, the one that crosses so slowly across the road and then you swerve to make sure you hit it and then a car coming the other way swerves to avoid you and goes off a cliff. And then that night you and your companion have the greatest sex of your lives because you're both sharing a secret. / It's a turtle, Jenna.
jokes.setup: Jenna is trying to make a metaphor about Thad coming out of his shell, but can't remember the animal
jokes.punchline: Her description of a 'turtle' involves vehicular manslaughter, road carnage, and post-crime bonding sex — all delivered as if this is a normal shared experience
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. What begins as an innocent 'what's that animal?' riddle escalates into a vivid scene of deliberate turtle homicide, a cliff-crash fatality, and then post-manslaughter intimacy — and Jenna delivers every step with dreamy nostalgia. The 'you and your companion' implies this has happened to her specifically. 'It's a turtle, Jenna' is the perfect deadpan puncture. This rivals the calibration anchors — it's original, perfectly structured, could ONLY be Jenna, and earns every escalating step.

jokes.text: We really gotta get all the furniture out of here? My aquarium guy's coming to see about turning this whole room into an aquarium. / Who's really in the aquarium? The fish or us?
jokes.setup: Thad is converting his living room into an aquarium
jokes.punchline: He poses the philosophical question of who is really 'in' the aquarium
jokes.explanation: A nerdy-billionaire joke: the room-as-aquarium is extravagant, and Thad's pseudo-profound question about who is 'really' in the aquarium reads as genuine nerd philosopher behavior. Mildly funny but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Unfortunately due to the Obama worldwide recession, there will be no Leap Day bonuses this year. Mean laughter, sound of a drink being poured. What are you writing now, you slack-jawed donkey?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is reading out a memo from Jack Donaghy to the staff
jokes.punchline: The memo includes stage directions ('mean laughter, sound of a drink being poured') and then Jack appears to be dictating in real-time, insulting whoever is transcribing it
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly structured meta-joke. The memo includes performance stage directions, which Jack presumably dictated expecting them to be performed — showing his total lack of awareness of how memos work OR his complete contempt for the staff. The snap to 'you slack-jawed donkey' as a live interjection is perfect escalation. Extremely quotable. Could only be Jack Donaghy.

jokes.text: A $50,000 Benihana gift card? / Right, I did an ad and insisted on being paid in Beni Bucks. / No sir, this card is only good through February 2012. / Any other year it'd be March already. But we found it today! It's a Leap Day miracle!
jokes.setup: Tracy discovers an expired Benihana gift card worth $50,000 — which he received as payment for an ad
jokes.punchline: In any other year the card would be expired (it expires in February), but because it's Leap Day they have one more day — calling it a 'Leap Day miracle'
jokes.explanation: A perfect 30 Rock Rube Goldberg joke. The setup layers two absurdities: Tracy getting paid in Benihana gift cards, and the card happening to expire on Feb 29. Then Leap Day makes the expired card valid. The logic is airtight and deliriously specific. 'Beni Bucks' is an inspired detail. The 'Leap Day miracle' tag uses the episode's mythology pay off a financial subplot. One of the tightest constructed jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Nothing's impossible on Leap Day. It's like I said in my cameo appearance in Leap Dave Williams: 'Gimme your wallet, old man!'
jokes.setup: Tracy rallies the team to spend $50,000 at Benihana
jokes.punchline: He cites his cameo in the fictional 'Leap Dave Williams' movie — and his cameo dialogue is a mugging threat to an old man
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Tracy had a cameo in the fictional holiday film AND that his cameo was threatening an old man for his wallet is a perfect Tracy Jordan joke. It expands the episode's fake mythology while being completely consistent with Tracy's character and career. The non-sequitur delivery sells it.

jokes.text: Following an unintentionally racist press conference... Help us to 'Whip' the competition. Kabletown shares down sharply...
jokes.setup: Jack holds a press conference to announce the 3-D Internet acquisition
jokes.punchline: His slogan 'Help us Whip the competition' (accompanied by gestures, presumably) reads as racist — causing the stock to drop
jokes.explanation: A darkly comic beat about corporate tone-deafness, delivered as a rapid news chyron cutaway. The joke trusts the audience to fill in what happened without showing it. Good economy.

jokes.text: Careful, sir, those leaves are poisonous. / You know the saying, 'rhubarb red, eat away, rhubarb green, don't eat them.' / Kenneth, I've watched Newt Gingrich eat a plate of ribs. I think my stomach can handle some rhubarb leaves.
jokes.setup: Kenneth warns Jack not to eat the rhubarb leaves
jokes.punchline: Jack dismisses the warning by invoking Newt Gingrich eating ribs as evidence of stomach fortitude
jokes.explanation: The Newt Gingrich detail is wonderfully specific — the image of Gingrich aggressively eating ribs as the gold standard of digestive toughness is both absurd and somehow totally believable. Jack's logic is impeccable within his worldview. Also sets up his later poisoning.

jokes.text: One of my birds is sick and I want to get home in time to baptize her.
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks how long Jack will need him today
jokes.punchline: He needs to get home to baptize his sick bird
jokes.explanation: Pure Kenneth Parcell. The combination of his rural religiosity and earnest animal care expressed as a baptism for a bird is perfectly calibrated absurdism. No other character on television would say this unironically.

jokes.text: Now, would you watch a television show... And I'm just spitballing here... Called Spitball?
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to brainstorm new shows to reverse his bad Leap Day
jokes.punchline: He casually invents a show called 'Spitball' while claiming to 'just be spitballing' — and seems genuinely excited by the name
jokes.explanation: A quick wordplay/meta joke — 'spitballing' an idea called 'Spitball.' The self-awareness of the verbal coincidence, delivered as a genuine pitch, is mildly clever. Quick and economical.

jokes.text: Sherry, I'm afraid something has come up at work and you'll have to stay late with Liddy. Just dab some scotch on your neck and make your eyes the color of a winter crystal so she'll think you're me.
jokes.setup: Jack calls the nanny to stay late with his daughter Liddy
jokes.punchline: His instructions for impersonating him involve scotch on the neck and 'winter crystal' eyes — implying his baby daughter can only identify him by scent and eye color, and the nanny can replicate those
jokes.explanation: 'Make your eyes the color of a winter crystal' is a genuinely poetic and strange image delivered as practical parenting advice. The joke layers Jack's absentee fatherhood, his vanity about his own features, and the absurd idea that these qualities can be faked. Nicely set up for the later Christmas Carol parody.

jokes.text: It's my, uh, D&D room. The gaming table comes up out of the floor. / Table! / Frak, I'm supposed to say 'floor' first.
jokes.setup: Thad is showing Liz and Jenna around his apartment
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates his D&D table that rises from the floor, but says 'Table!' prematurely and has to correct himself, revealing he has practiced this reveal
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed nerd-billionaire joke. Thad has clearly practiced his cool apartment reveal, but blows it by saying 'Table!' at the wrong time. The use of 'Frak' (Battlestar Galactica profanity) as his expletive of choice is perfect character detail. The joke implies hours of solo rehearsal for this moment.

jokes.text: I have been in love with you since college. Watching you every night on that stage and realizing my dad was wrong. I do like girls.
jokes.setup: Thad tells Liz this whole party and apartment was for her — a grand romantic confession
jokes.punchline: His love for Liz 'proved' he was straight — implying he wasn't sure before and his dad didn't think so either
jokes.explanation: A dark-ish character joke hiding in the middle of an earnest confession. 'My dad was wrong. I do like girls.' is delivered as an aside that recontextualizes the grand romance — Thad isn't just lovesick, he was also going through a sexual identity crisis, using Liz Lemon as evidence. Good misdirection within a romantic scene.

jokes.text: That is why it's called Xaro. In Game of Thrones, Xaro is a rich merchant prince who wishes to acquaint himself with the mother of dragons.
jokes.setup: Thad reveals his company Xaro (which Jack just bought) was named after a Game of Thrones character
jokes.punchline: The company Kabletown just acquired for a fortune was named because of a nerd's crush — and the Game of Thrones parallel is Thad seeing himself as the merchant prince pursuing a dragon queen
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Thad's romantic scheme extends all the way to naming his billion-dollar company after a TV character, the GoT reference reveals his self-image (dragon-courting prince), and it retroactively makes Jack's acquisition absurd. Good layered writing.

jokes.text: Great, well... Scooby Doo! [Liz runs away]
jokes.setup: Thad makes a massive romantic declaration
jokes.punchline: Liz's response is to yell 'Scooby Doo!' and flee — presumably invoking the cartoon to signal absurdity/panic as an escape mechanism
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Scooby Doo!' as a flight response is pure Liz Lemon panic — she uses pop culture as punctuation when words fail her. Quick, specific, and very in-character.

jokes.text: Liz, wait! $10 million! / I want you to take my virginity on leap night for $10 million. / Fine, 20. / No, Thad, I... / Don't answer yet. I mean, okay, unless you were gonna say yes. / No, you heard me say no. / Don't answer yet. / Don't answer yet.
jokes.setup: Thad propositions Liz sexually for money
jokes.punchline: He immediately doubles the offer, then panics mid-no, saying 'don't answer yet' after she's clearly already answered, repeating it desperately
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic escalation. The rhythm of 'Don't answer yet / don't answer yet' repeated after she's clearly said no is perfectly timed cringe. The self-correction ('I mean, okay, unless you were gonna say yes') shows Thad's panic in real-time. The jump from $10M to $20M in a single breath is a great character beat.

jokes.text: Son of a glub.
jokes.setup: Thad is frustrated after Liz runs away
jokes.punchline: His expletive is 'son of a glub' — a PG underwater-themed profanity
jokes.explanation: 'Son of a glub' is a bespoke expletive that implies an aquatic existence — consistent with Thad's love of his would-be aquarium room and generally odd biology (he had skin tags over his eyes). The invented word is memorable and economical.

jokes.text: Mr. Jordan, you'll never spend all this by midnight. You appeared in that ad for nothing. / Well, the joke's on you because that commercial never aired for unexplained reasons.
jokes.setup: Dotcom doubts Tracy can spend $50,000 at Benihana
jokes.punchline: Tracy claims victory because the commercial never aired, but this actually means he did the ad for nothing AND now can't spend the gift cards — a double loss he's framing as a win
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic inversion — presenting a double failure as 'the joke being on' his critic — is classic Tracy Jordan. 'For unexplained reasons' is a perfectly economy detail implying something chaotic happened that no one is explaining.

jokes.text: I just touched the table again. God, you call for help! I'll just put my head on the table for a second.
jokes.setup: Thad is still dealing with the rising D&D table in his apartment
jokes.punchline: He keeps accidentally triggering the table, then gives up and rests his head on it
jokes.explanation: A running gag callback to the D&D table — it's funny but lighter than the original. The escalation of him giving up and resting on the offending table is a nice physical button.

jokes.text: You know, I just kept seeing your face. Also, I have too much dignity.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Criss she couldn't go through with Thad's proposition
jokes.punchline: She leads with 'I kept seeing your face' (romantic) then immediately adds 'Also, I have too much dignity' — the 'also' implying these are equal considerations
jokes.explanation: The 'also' is doing all the work — it deflates the romantic moment by making dignity a co-equal reason to the face-seeing. Very Liz Lemon: she WANTS to be romantic but her neurotic pragmatism keeps punctuating it. Good structure and character integration.

jokes.text: So another woman? / Victoria's Secret model.
jokes.setup: Criss asks if another woman took Thad's offer
jokes.punchline: It was a Victoria's Secret model
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed punchline. The specific 'Victoria's Secret model' confirms Jenna's earlier prediction about beautiful women arriving and is delivered with perfect economy. Liz says it completely neutrally.

jokes.text: It's Leap Day. Real life is for March. / Nothing that happens on Leap Day counts.
jokes.setup: Liz is hesitant about doing something crazy
jokes.punchline: Both Jenna AND Criss independently invoke the same Leap Day philosophy — 'real life is for March' / 'nothing on Leap Day counts'
jokes.explanation: The joke is that both characters say almost exactly the same thing, confirming that this is the universal Leap Day philosophy — Liz is truly isolated in not understanding it. 'Real life is for March' is a highly quotable, elegant expression of the episode's central absurdist premise.

jokes.text: It looks like we've got a slut-off on our hands.
jokes.setup: Both Jenna and Liz seem to be considering Thad's proposition
jokes.punchline: Jenna assesses the situation with the clinical term 'slut-off'
jokes.explanation: Pure Jenna. 'Slut-off' is an invented compound noun delivered with sportscaster calm. The economy is excellent — two words summarize a complex situation. Very in-character and quotable.

jokes.text: We've only spent $6000. We should just give up. / Never. / We can't keep eating! / Lutz's shirt button popped off and hit Cerie. It counts as us touching.
jokes.setup: The TGS writers are failing to eat $50,000 worth of Benihana food
jokes.punchline: Dotcom reports Lutz's shirt button launched off from overeating and struck Cerie — which counts as physical contact in their desperate accounting
jokes.explanation: The image of Lutz bursting a shirt button from overeating and the button ricocheting into Cerie is both visually funny and satisfyingly specific. 'It counts as us touching' introduces a bizarre metric of progress. Lutz being the one to burst is perfect casting within the writers' room ensemble.

jokes.text: Everybody's always telling me not to get paid in gift cards. Angie, my lawyer, my imaginary friend, Dotcom. / Tray, I'm real. I moved your furniture.
jokes.setup: Tracy lists people who have warned him against gift card compensation
jokes.punchline: Dotcom is listed alongside Tracy's imaginary friend — and has to assert his own reality, citing furniture-moving as proof
jokes.explanation: Brilliant. Dotcom being grouped with an imaginary friend and having to prove his existence by citing physical labor is one of the best Dotcom/Tracy jokes in the episode. 'I moved your furniture' as existential proof is both pathetic and deeply sad. The delivery must be perfectly deadpan to land. This is genuinely exceptional character comedy.

jokes.text: One Leap Day when I was a kid, the Harlem River froze, and I decided to cross it carrying my brick collection. / I told him not to. / No one can hear you, Dotcom. / Then I fell through the ice. They still don't know who pulled me out. / I did. / Charlie Rangel gave me a medal.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells his Leap Day memory to inspire the group
jokes.punchline: Three-part escalation: (1) carrying bricks across frozen river, (2) Dotcom's advice ignored/inaudible, (3) Dotcom rescues him but gets no credit while Charlie Rangel gets a medal
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest extended jokes. Tracy's absurd childhood story gains layers: the brick collection, Dotcom's advice being 'inaudible,' Dotcom's rescue being completely unacknowledged ('They still don't know who pulled me out' / 'I did'), and the punchline that Charlie Rangel got a medal for it. Each beat escalates the tragedy of Dotcom's relationship with Tracy while being hilarious. 'No one can hear you, Dotcom' when Dotcom is standing right there is exceptional.

jokes.text: You're famous. I have screen grabs of all your nip s.
jokes.setup: Thad approaches Jenna at the party
jokes.punchline: His opening line is that he has saved screenshots of her visible nipples
jokes.explanation: A perfect encapsulation of Thad as a max-creep nerd. The casual admission of having an organized collection of celebrity 'nip slips' is disturbing and funny. Jenna's non-reaction is implied cringe gold.

jokes.text: What was the dance that Rolf did for Liesl? Did it go like this? / Yes. / That's it. That's how Rolf danced.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks Thad to recall the dance from Sound of Music, using it as a distraction
jokes.punchline: Thad confirms Jenna's dance is correct, then Jenna uses it to dance him away — she's manipulating him with his own Sound of Music nostalgia
jokes.explanation: A callback to the Sound of Music setup that pays off cleverly — Jenna uses Thad's theater nostalgia as a manipulation tool to steer him away from Liz. The visual of them doing the Rolf dance is implied physical comedy. Good callback construction.

jokes.text: Right now, there are models waking up from their coke binges, multi-ethnic bartenders with daddy issues, former ballerinas who had to quit because their boobs got too big. They're gonna hear about the horny billionaire, and Thad's gonna forget all about his little crush. They're coming, Liz. Click click. That's their stilettos. Click click.
jokes.setup: Jenna is advising Liz to move fast on Thad's offer
jokes.punchline: She enumerates the exact types of women who will arrive for a 'horny billionaire,' ending with the sound of approaching stilettos: 'Click click. That's their stilettos. Click click.'
jokes.explanation: One of Jenna's best speeches in the episode. The taxonomy of gold-digger archetypes ('multi-ethnic bartenders with daddy issues,' 'former ballerinas who had to quit because their boobs got too big') is specific and inspired. The onomatopoeia of 'Click click. That's their stilettos.' as an auditory countdown is brilliant — urgent, absurd, and totally Jenna. Extremely quotable, perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Please get better, sir. I've dug too many graves.
jokes.setup: Jack has collapsed from eating poisonous rhubarb leaves and Kenneth tends to him
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's bedside plea reveals he has a history of digging graves — stated with utter matter-of-fact sincerity
jokes.explanation: Six words, devastating. 'I've dug too many graves' is Kenneth Parcell at his most unsettling — his rural past and apparent immortality (a running show mythology) collide in what is both genuine concern and a casual confession of repeated death-adjacent labor. The economy is near-perfect. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Why the long face, son? / I do have a long, elegant face, thank you, but I can't enjoy your compliment, because I'm sad.
jokes.setup: An old man asks Kenneth why he has a long face (idiom for being sad)
jokes.punchline: Kenneth takes it literally, acknowledges his actual long face, thanks the man, then circles back to being sad
jokes.explanation: A classic idiom-taken-literally joke but executed with excellent character integration. Kenneth's earnest self-description ('long, elegant face') and his attempt to be polite while grieving is perfectly Kenneth. The triple beat — literalism, gratitude, return to sadness — is well-structured.

jokes.text: I reckon you may be right. Leap Day William's probably just a tall tale told to kids to help sell candy. But this old fool still believes he exists, right here, inside all of us. / I am always coughing up blood. Could that be Leap Day William trying to get out?
jokes.setup: An old man offers Kenneth folksy wisdom about believing in Leap Day William
jokes.punchline: Kenneth interprets 'William lives inside all of us' literally — wondering if his blood-coughing is William trying to escape his body
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's literal interpretation of metaphor combined with the alarming confession that he 'is always coughing up blood' is a great Kenneth joke. The image of Leap Day William violently trying to exit Kenneth's body through blood is wonderfully grotesque. Also hints at Kenneth's supernatural nature (a recurring show mythology).

jokes.text: Thanks. Nice costume, by the way. / Right, costume.
jokes.setup: The old man has been giving Kenneth Leap Day William-style wisdom
jokes.punchline: Kenneth says 'nice costume,' and the old man confirms 'right, costume' — heavily implying he actually IS Leap Day William but going along with the cover
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical magical realism beat. The old man's 'Right, costume' pause and delivery confirms without confirming — the show's mythology is treated as real within the fiction. Six words do everything needed. Great rewatch value.

jokes.text: So, what should we do now? / Stop pressuring me. What are you? An intercourse monster?
jokes.setup: Liz and Thad are alone and the situation is awkward
jokes.punchline: Thad's response to a neutral question is to accuse Liz of being an 'intercourse monster'
jokes.explanation: 'Intercourse monster' is one of the most quotable coinages in the episode. It captures Thad's paradox perfectly: he propositioned Liz for money but is terrified of actual intimacy. Using 'intercourse' (clinical, distancing) rather than any colloquial term is perfect for a virgin nerd. Highly original and very funny.

jokes.text: Is sex like when the Na'vi intertwine their hair braids? / Sure. Yeah, Thad, that's exactly what it's like.
jokes.setup: Thad nervously asks about sex
jokes.punchline: His mental model of sex is the Avatar Na'vi hair-braid connection, and Liz just agrees to end the conversation
jokes.explanation: A perfect virgin-nerd joke. Thad's conceptual framework for sex comes from Avatar fan theory — the Na'vi neural link (a genuinely intimate but non-sexual act in the film) as his sex analogue. Liz's exasperated agreement is the perfect button. Extremely character-specific.

jokes.text: Aw, damn it. Hot bitches. [Models arrive]
jokes.setup: Jenna predicted the models would arrive; Liz is trying to get Thad to go through with their encounter
jokes.punchline: Liz's defeated reaction to seeing beautiful women arrive, exactly as predicted
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Jenna's earlier prediction. Liz's two-word defeated reaction — said with total matter-of-factness — is funnier than a longer complaint would be. The callback structure works well.

jokes.text: Kenneth, is that me? / I'm not Kenneth. I'm the spirit of Leap Day. Welcome to your Leap Day past.
jokes.setup: Jack, sick from the rhubarb leaves, has a Christmas Carol-style vision
jokes.punchline: Kenneth appears as 'the spirit of Leap Day' — an obvious direct parody of A Christmas Carol, with Leap Day substituted
jokes.explanation: The Leap Day Christmas Carol parody is a great structural choice — it's a known framework being applied to a fake holiday, and Kenneth as the ghost is perfect casting. The show commits fully to the bit.

jokes.text: Jackie, we can't go to the parade today. I got called into work... at the hospital... where I'm a nurse.
jokes.setup: Young Jack's mother explains why they can't go to the Leap Day parade
jokes.punchline: She identifies herself as a nurse with odd pauses — as if she's making it up on the spot or it's surprising that she's a nurse
jokes.explanation: The comedic hesitations in 'at the hospital... where I'm a nurse' are funny — they read as either improvised justification or genuine surprise at her own occupation. A smaller joke within the Christmas Carol sequence.

jokes.text: Good. Cry. Let your sadness form a hole inside you that can only be filled with money.
jokes.setup: Kenneth shows Jack a memory of a sad childhood Leap Day
jokes.punchline: The 'spirit' encourages the young Jack's sadness as the origin of his capitalist drive: 'Let your sadness form a hole that can only be filled with money'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes and a strong candidate for the series. 'Let your sadness form a hole inside you that can only be filled with money' is a perfectly written line that functions simultaneously as: (1) a devastating psychological insight into Jack Donaghy, (2) a dark parody of Christmas Carol ghost guidance, and (3) a quotable stand-alone aphorism. The economy is superb, the character integration is total — this is the origin story of Jack Donaghy in one sentence. Rivals the calibration anchors.

jokes.text: Of course we're going to the parade today, Jackie. But you can't have candy and cigarettes without a few tears first.
jokes.setup: Young Jack's mother relents and agrees to take him to the Leap Day parade
jokes.punchline: The Leap Day tradition apparently involves giving children 'candy and cigarettes' — and the tears are a prerequisite
jokes.explanation: Adding cigarettes to the Leap Day children's gift canon (alongside candy) is an excellent dark addition to the mythology. The casual '1950s parenting' of giving kids cigarettes, framed as holiday tradition, is very funny.

jokes.text: When did we stop giving children cigarettes? It's the liberal war on Leap Day.
jokes.setup: Jack watches the childhood memory of receiving cigarettes for Leap Day
jokes.punchline: He frames the end of giving children cigarettes as a liberal attack on Leap Day traditions
jokes.explanation: 'The liberal war on Leap Day' is a perfect coinage — it directly parodies 'the war on Christmas' rhetoric while revealing Jack's politics and his nostalgic conservatism. 'When did we stop giving children cigarettes?' delivered with genuine bewilderment is exceptional. Very quotable and highly character-specific.

jokes.text: Welcome to Leap Day present. / Okay, I'll change my eye color, but it seems like a waste of voodoo.
jokes.setup: Kenneth takes Jack to 'Leap Day present' — showing the nanny following Jack's instructions to impersonate him
jokes.punchline: The nanny grumbles that changing her eye color is 'a waste of voodoo' — implying voodoo is a real and finite resource in her life
jokes.explanation: A brilliant payoff to the earlier Jack-eye-color instruction. The callback reveals the nanny actually USES voodoo, and her complaint is about resource management rather than ethics. 'A waste of voodoo' is an extraordinary seven-word joke. Excellent economy and originality.

jokes.text: Five leap days from now. That's Liddy. I assume this is her horse stable and that she's hammering that nail as a funny joke. / No, Mr. Donaghy. She's doing Habitat for Humanity. After you missed all her leap days, she started experimenting with liberalism.
jokes.setup: Kenneth shows Jack the future — Liddy as a young adult doing manual labor
jokes.punchline: Jack assumes it's an ironic rich-girl pose, but it's genuine liberal volunteerism caused by his absence — 'she started experimenting with liberalism'
jokes.explanation: Jack's worst nightmare is his daughter becoming a liberal — and the show frames liberalism as a rebellious 'experiment' like drugs or a bad relationship. 'She started experimenting with liberalism' is a wonderfully specific and pointed satirical line. Jack's defensive assumption that the hammering is 'a funny joke' is also perfect denial comedy.

jokes.text: Kenneth, I want you to go to Citarella and buy the biggest rhubarb there is. The one that's as big as me, sir? That's the one. But first, you take Rebecca Birdstein to the vet.
jokes.setup: Jack, moved by the Christmas Carol vision, decides to make amends
jokes.punchline: His grand gesture involves a specific giant rhubarb AND he remembers Kenneth's sick bird before his own redemption errand
jokes.explanation: A nice triple callback: the rhubarb running gag (which poisoned Jack), Kenneth's sick bird, and the Christmas Carol 'big turkey' tradition all merge. 'The one that's as big as me, sir?' is a good Kenneth line. The generosity of remembering Rebecca Birdstein first is a warm character beat.

jokes.text: What a Mitzvah. / Merry Leap Day, sir. / Merry Leap Day to us all!
jokes.setup: Jack's Scrooge-like redemption arc concludes
jokes.punchline: The Christmas Carol ending is transposed onto Leap Day — 'Merry Leap Day to us all' as a direct riff on 'God bless us, every one'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying parody conclusion to the Christmas Carol subplot. Jack's 'Merry Leap Day to us all!' with presumably Donaghy-esque gusto is the expected button and it lands.

jokes.text: Liz, why don't you go and... Get you and Karolina some drinks? / Okay, fine. / Looks like this time the male will be in the Czech. That kind of wit is a thing she will never give you.
jokes.setup: Thad has chosen the Victoria's Secret model (named Karolina, implying Czech/Slovak origin) over Liz
jokes.punchline: Thad makes a pun: 'the male will be in the Czech' (the male = Thad; Czech = check/Karolina's nationality) and self-congratulates it as wit Liz could never offer
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever pun that Thad is correct to be proud of — 'male in the Czech' works on multiple levels (he's pursuing a Czech model, and the 'check' pun implies he's cashing in on his bet). His self-satisfaction in noting 'that kind of wit is a thing she will never give you' is nerd-victory comedy. One of the better puns in the episode.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz. A gym teacher on a sex tour of Indonesia called. He wants his shirt back.
jokes.setup: The model sees Liz's casual shirt and delivers an insult
jokes.punchline: The insult is that Liz dresses like a gym teacher on a sex tour of Indonesia — which implies a very specific and unflattering mental image
jokes.explanation: A very well-constructed insult — the specificity of 'gym teacher on a sex tour of Indonesia' is what elevates it from a generic clothing burn. The joke paints a vivid, unflattering picture with excellent economy. Liz's acknowledgment ('Okay, that's solid') is a nice meta-beat.

jokes.text: Okay, that's solid, Kurkova. That's a good burn.
jokes.setup: The model insults Liz's appearance
jokes.punchline: Liz acknowledges the burn is genuinely good — she can't help but appreciate well-crafted comedy even at her own expense
jokes.explanation: Liz complimenting the person insulting her is perfect Liz Lemon — she's too honest and comedy-aware to pretend it wasn't good. The acknowledgment is funnier than a defensive response would be.

jokes.text: Remember where I came from. / But we all came from the sea. Sea? Like the letter 'C', which is part of the alphabet. Alphabet soup. Soup kitchen. Kitchen... / No, no, don't keep going. / The kitchen debate with Richard Nixon. Richard M. Nixon. The M-train. Soul train. Chicken soup for the soul. Chicken soup. Soup kitchen. / This is a Leap Day miracle!
jokes.setup: Tracy tries to recall the old man's wisdom to find meaning for the leftover food
jokes.punchline: He free-associates through a chain of word-logic that loops back to 'soup kitchen' — which he decides is a Leap Day miracle, even though the logic is completely deranged
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Tracy Jordan stream-of-consciousness set piece. The word-association chain (sea → C → alphabet → alphabet soup → soup kitchen → kitchen debate → Nixon → M-train → Soul Train → Chicken Soup for the Soul → chicken soup → soup kitchen) is both completely deranged AND has its own internal logic. Dotcom's exasperated 'No, no, don't keep going' perfectly mirrors the audience's laughter. Tracy's triumphant 'This is a Leap Day miracle!' upon arriving at 'soup kitchen' (which is actually useful for the leftover food) is the payoff. Outstanding.

jokes.text: Merry Leap Day, tourists. / Merry Leap Day, closeted gay guys meeting in the city.
jokes.setup: Tracy is distributing food to people in what appears to be a park or public space
jokes.punchline: His Leap Day greetings are targeted at specific, identified groups — especially 'closeted gay guys meeting in the city'
jokes.explanation: Tracy's specific acknowledgment of 'closeted gay guys meeting in the city' as a distinct category to greet is funny in its specificity and matter-of-factness. A quick character beat.

jokes.text: Seriously, 20 million bucks? I would sleep with Thad Warmald for that. / Couldn't go through with it. You know, I just kept seeing your face. Also, I have too much dignity. / So another woman? / Victoria's Secret model. / Feast, homeless, feast!
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are having an intimate moment about the Thad situation
jokes.punchline: Tracy interrupts by commanding homeless people to feast — completely shattering the romantic moment
jokes.explanation: 'Feast, homeless, feast!' is a perfect Tracy Jordan command — the word order, the inverted repetition of 'feast,' and the sudden intrusion into a tender scene is beautifully timed. It's also the payoff of the Benihana subplot. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I saved Leap Day! And connected with my son! And I solved the big case from earlier!
jokes.setup: Tracy celebrates his Leap Day achievements
jokes.punchline: He lists three triumphs including 'I solved the big case from earlier' — which was never mentioned in the episode, implying an entire subplot happened off-screen
jokes.explanation: The genius of 'I solved the big case from earlier' is that it references a plot thread that never existed in this episode — implying Tracy has an entire detective subplot we never saw. It's a perfect meta joke about TV storytelling and Tracy's inscrutable life. Highly original and very quotable.

jokes.text: Well, I guess we all learned something tonight about love and friendship, about taking chances, about the true meaning of Leap Day. But these lessons aren't good just for every four years. No, they're good every year. Because we should live every day as if it's Leap Day, and every Leap Day as if it's your last.
jokes.setup: The episode concludes with an earnest holiday moral in the style of a TV special
jokes.punchline: The lesson of 'live every day as if it's Leap Day' is absurd — it's telling people to behave as if normal consequences don't apply every single day
jokes.explanation: The closing moral is a parody of holiday special wrap-ups, but the specific lesson is deliberately nonsensical — 'live every day as Leap Day' would mean ignoring all consequences every day, which is chaos. The show is winking at the audience while delivering a straight-faced lesson.

jokes.text: And if you should ever see an old man in a blue suit busting out of the middle of the ocean, take the time to say howdy. It might just be worth your while.
jokes.setup: The closing narration of the episode
jokes.punchline: The final image of the episode's mythology — Leap Day William bursting from the ocean — is delivered as sincere holiday advice
jokes.explanation: A satisfying mythological button to the episode. 'Busting out of the middle of the ocean' as a sincere holiday image, delivered in the style of a Christmas special sign-off, is the right tone to end the Leap Day world-building. 'Take the time to say howdy' is a charming absurdist detail.

tmdb_overview: Jack learns to appreciate Leap Day while Tracy takes the writers to a restaurant to spend an almost-expired gift card. Liz helps Jenna seduce an internet billionaire.
insight: Absurdist holiday special sustains 2.6 jokes per minute across 57 gags.
